story: Lofotodden is a landscape found in few other places in the world: high, narrow ranges of sharp peaks standing straight out of the open sea. On Moskenesøya and Flakstadøya the mountains form the mightiest stretch of the Lofoten Wall, cut so deeply by fjords and sounds that the land barely holds together. During the last ice age the great inland ice only briefly rode over these mountains; small local glaciers survived here for long periods instead, and they carved the peaks, ridges, deep cirques and narrow fjords. The highest summit is Hermannsdalstinden, 1,029 metres, west of Reine.

The cliffs and islets are important nesting grounds for seabirds — shag, kittiwake, black guillemot and Arctic skua — and golden eagles, white-tailed eagles and several falcons breed here too. Because Lofoten was freed from the ice early, Norway's mountain flora may have its oldest footholds here. On the strandflats along the coast grow red-listed habitats: old hay meadows and sand dunes with an unusual flora.

People have lived on this coast for some 6,000 years, and the park is rich in cultural remains, from Stone Age house sites onwards. The best known is Kollhellaren in Refsvika, a cave some 115 metres long whose walls carry about 30 figures painted around 3,000 years ago. Archaeology students noticed them in 1987, though people in Refsvika had long known the cave itself. Today it can be visited only with an authorised guide.

Lofotodden National Park was established on 22 June 2018 to keep a large area with a distinctive natural heritage — landscape without heavy intervention, habitats, species and geology — together with its cultural heritage. It covers about 99 square kilometres in Moskenes and Flakstad, about 13 of them sea. It is also one of the easier Norwegian parks to reach, with good bus and ferry connections, and many of its best views need no summit at all: walk barefoot on the beaches, or see the mountains from the water on a guided boat or kayak trip.
howItWorks: Norway's right to roam, allemannsretten, applies here as on any uncultivated land: you may walk and pitch a tent without asking, provided you camp at least 150 metres from the nearest house or cabin and leave no trace. From 15 April to 15 September it is illegal across Norway to light a fire in or near woodland. Dogs must be kept on a lead nationwide from 1 April to 20 August.

The park's regulation protects the landscape from all works and forbids removing larger stones and breaking out rock, minerals or fossils. Motor traffic is banned on land and fresh water and in the air below 300 metres, though boats may use the sea. Drones, motor-driven model aircraft and the like are banned unless the management authority gives permission. Bicycles on bare ground and organised riding are allowed only on roads and paths, and cycling is not allowed at all on the paths from Bunesfjorden to Bunes and from Torsfjorden to Kvalvika. Animals and their nests are protected from disturbance; wood may be used carefully for a fire.

Lofotodden is popular and fragile, and litter must go home with you. Fishing, hunting and the old use of the strandflats for grazing go on under the general rules. Many organised trips — overnight tent trips, larger or repeated groups, and guided climbing, paddling or cycling — need permission from the national park board; check its rules for groups before you go.

sightNotes.poi-no-lofotodden-bunes: A broad white beach on the outer coast below steep peaks, reached on foot over the low pass Einangen from Vindstad, which most visitors reach by passenger boat from Reine.
sightNotes.poi-no-lofotodden-kvalvika: A beach in a cove on the open Atlantic side of Moskenesøya, just outside the park, reached on foot from Fredvang or Innersand. No cycling on the path from Torsfjorden.
sightNotes.poi-no-lofotodden-ryten: The 543-metre summit above Kvalvika on Moskenesøya, a gentle walk that ends abruptly above the open sea.
sightNotes.poi-no-lofotodden-hermannsdalstinden: At 1,029 metres the highest peak on Moskenesøya, about 6.5 kilometres west of Reine.
sightNotes.poi-no-lofotodden-helvetestinden: The polished 602-metre peak rising above the beach at Bunes.
sightNotes.poi-no-lofotodden-agvatnet: A lake above Å at the southern end of the island, just outside the park, with the sandy Melkarsanden on its shore.
sightNotes.poi-no-lofotodden-kollhellaren-refsvika: A cave 115 metres long with about 30 figures painted some 3,000 years ago. Visits only with an authorised guide.

entrances: Reine, with the visitor centre, and Å at the end of the E10
Vindstad — for the walk over to Bunes
Fredvang and Innersand in Flakstad — for Kvalvika and Ryten; parking is paid and roadside parking is not allowed
planYourVisit.reservations: There is no entry reservation or permit. A visit to Kollhellaren must be booked with an authorised guide.
permits: Drones may be flown only with permission from the management authority
Many organised trips and all larger events need permission from the national park board; small day groups may not — check its rules for groups
camping: Wild camping under the right to roam, at least 150 metres from houses and cabins; leave no trace on the beaches
No fires in or near woodland from 15 April to 15 September
lodging: Lodging in the villages along the E10, such as Reine and Å

chronology.text: People settle this coast; Stone Age house sites survive in the park.
Human figures are painted on the walls of Kollhellaren in Refsvika.
Archaeology students record the paintings in Kollhellaren.
Lofotodden National Park is established on 22 June.

safety: Paths are steep and exposed, and many cross loose scree or wet rock. Wear proper boots and turn back if the weather closes in.
The open Atlantic beaches have strong currents and cold water. Swim only in calm conditions, close to shore.
Weather on the outer coast changes fast, with sudden wind, rain and fog. Carry warm, windproof clothing even on a fine summer day.
Keep away from cliff edges: the turf and rock at the top are often loose.
regulations: No drones without permission, and no motor traffic on land or fresh water.
No cycling on the paths from Bunesfjorden to Bunes and from Torsfjorden to Kvalvika; elsewhere, bicycles only on roads and paths.
Do not move larger stones or break out rock, minerals or fossils.
Take all rubbish home, and keep dogs on a lead from 1 April to 20 August.

weather: Lofoten's climate is far milder than its latitude suggests, but it is wet, windy and changeable, and the weather on the outer coast can turn within the hour. Summer brings the midnight sun and the best walking; snow can lie on the peaks into early summer. In autumn and winter storms sweep the outer coast and daylight is short.
directions: The car ferry from Bodø to Moskenes takes about three and a half hours. By road, the E10 runs the length of Lofoten to Å; the park lies about 40 kilometres south-west of Leknes, which has an airport. Buses run along the E10 to Reine and Å. Check Entur for ferry and bus timetables.
